summary: Defines the MIME Multipart/Related content type, used for compound documents in which parts such as images belong together with a main part, and gives examples of its use.

plainLanguage.summary: Multipart/Related packages a main document with the other MIME parts it needs, such as images. The type parameter names the main part's media type, and the start parameter can identify that part.

questions: what is the start parameter in multipart/related
what is a content-id in mime
subtitle: A MIME container for a document and the parts it needs to make sense.

tldr.problem: Some documents depend on several related MIME parts, so displaying each part alone does not show the complete object.
tldr.mechanism: Multipart/Related groups the parts, identifies the root part by position or content-ID, and declares the root's media type with a required type parameter.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2387 replaces RFC 2112 with a shared format for compound objects. A user agent that does not recognize the subtype treats it as Multipart/Mixed.

today: RFC 2387 is a Proposed Standard published in August 1998 and obsoletes RFC 2112. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Multipart/Related Exists
sections.content:
RFC 2387 defines Multipart/Related for compound objects made from MIME body parts that make sense only together. Before this subtype, each new compound object tended to define its own multipart subtype.

The application that handles the compound object decides how to process or display its parts. The type's parameters identify the root part and provide information the application may need.
sections.plainLanguage: Multipart/Related groups parts that must be handled together. The application that understands the object decides how to use each part.

sections.title: The Root and Its Parameters
sections.content:
The required type parameter gives the media type of the root body part. This lets a user agent identify the object's type without inspecting the body; if the parameter conflicts with the root part's Content-Type, the RFC leaves behavior undefined.

The optional start parameter identifies the root by its content-ID. If it is absent, the first body part is the root. The optional start-info parameter carries a string or points by content-ID to another MIME entity; the application specification defines how to interpret it.
sections.plainLanguage: The required type parameter names the main part's media type. The optional start parameter identifies that part; without it, the first part is the root.

sections.title: Parameter Syntax
sections.content:
The parameters can appear in any order. The type value is a media type and subtype separated by a slash; start contains a message ID; and start-info is a message-ID list or a token or quoted string.

Values usually need quotation because message IDs contain special characters and the slash in a media type is special. A start-info value whose first non-space character is an opening angle bracket is treated as a reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The parameters may appear in any order, but their values have different forms. Quotation marks are usually needed around values containing special characters.

sections.title: Content-Disposition and Older User Agents
sections.content:
A body part may include Content-Disposition to suggest inline display or an attachment and to provide a filename. A user agent that does not recognize Multipart/Related treats it as Multipart/Mixed and may use those suggestions.

A user agent that does recognize Multipart/Related follows the application that processes the compound object and ignores the part's disposition type, because that hint could conflict with the object's own rules. The application may use a filename if its specification allows it.
sections.plainLanguage: An older user agent can treat the parts as a mixed collection and use their display hints. A user agent that understands Multipart/Related follows the compound object's processing rules instead.

sections.title: What User Agents Provide
sections.content:
A user agent that does not recognize Multipart/Related treats the entity as Multipart/Mixed. One that recognizes the subtype but cannot process its type should let the user suppress the whole entity.

A MIME user agent must give the processing application each body and its Content-* headers, the Multipart/Related parameters, and the mapping between local filenames, headers, and content-IDs. Nested Multipart/Related entities are processed as though they were being stored.
sections.plainLanguage: The application needs every body part, its headers, the container parameters, and the content-ID to local-file mapping. If a user agent cannot process the object's type, it should offer to suppress the whole object.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says that security considerations for Multipart/Related are identical to those of the underlying content type. The referenced type determines the relevant security issues.

The registration also states that multipart content types cannot have content encodings. It does not define a separate security mechanism for the container.
sections.plainLanguage: Multipart/Related does not define separate security protections. Its security considerations depend on the content type of the compound object.
